claim: Detecting causal relations structures our perception of events in the world.
source: Detecting causal relations structures our perception of events in the world.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about causal perception.

claim: After prolonged exposure to causal launch events defined by a particular set of features, observers were less likely to see causal launches in subsequent ambiguous test events than before adaptation.
source: After prolonged exposure to causal launch events (the adaptor) defined by a particular set of features (i.e. a particular motion direction, motion speed, or feature conjunction), observers were less likely to see causal launches in subsequent ambiguous test events than before adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the adaptation protocol described in the manuscript.

claim: Adaptation was contingent on the causal impression in launches as demonstrated by a lack of adaptation in non-causal control events.
source: Crucially, adaptation was contingent on the causal impression in launches as demonstrated by a lack of adaptation in non-causal control events.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing launch events to slip events (non-causal control).

claim: Processing in specialized (as opposed to generalized) visual routines predicts that the transfer of visual adaptation depends on the feature similarity of the adaptor and the test event.
source: Processing in specialized (as opposed to generalized) visual routines predicts that the transfer of visual adaptation depends on the feature similarity of the adaptor and the test event.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on inference about how specialized vs. generalized visual routines would function.

claim: The negative aftereffects do not transfer to unadapted launch directions.
source: We show that the negative aftereffects do not transfer to unadapted launch directions but do transfer to launch events of different speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing direction-specific adaptation.

claim: The negative aftereffects do transfer to launch events of different speeds.
source: We show that the negative aftereffects do not transfer to unadapted launch directions but do transfer to launch events of different speeds.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 showing speed-invariant adaptation.

claim: The adaptation transferred across colors if the test event had the same motion direction as the adaptor.
source: We found that the adaptation transferred across colors if the test event had the same motion direction as the adaptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3 using colored discs.

claim: Visual adaptation revealed specialized visual routines that are tuned to a launch's motion direction.
source: In summary, visual adaptation allowed us to carve out a visual feature space underlying the perception of causality and revealed specialized visual routines that are tuned to a launch's motion direction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data across all three experiments.

claim: Proposed theories regarding our understanding of causal sensory interactions vary considerably, proposing purely perceptual, abstract probabilistic, or cognitive mechanisms.
source: The proposed theories regarding our understanding of causal sensory interactions vary considerably, proposing purely perceptual (Michotte, 1963; Scholl and Tremoulet, 2000), abstract probabilistic (Sanborn et al., 2013), or cognitive mechanisms (Rips, 2011; Weir, 1978; White, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple theoretical frameworks in the literature.

claim: The proposed theories are neither mutually exclusive nor do they make distinct predictions and they are, therefore, hard to distinguish.
source: These are neither mutually exclusive nor do they make distinct predictions and they are, therefore, hard to distinguish (Rips, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rips (2011) discussing the difficulty of distinguishing between theories.

claim: Adaptation is a powerful behavioral tool for discovering and dissecting a visual mechanism.
source: Adaptation is a powerful behavioral tool for discovering and dissecting a visual mechanism (Kohn, 2007; Webster, 2015) that provides an intriguing testing ground for the perceptual roots of causality.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on visual adaptation methods.

claim: Perceptual accounts of causal understanding posit the existence of visual routines—local, semi-independent operations that can engage mid- and higher-level processes.
source: Perceptual accounts of causal understanding posit the existence of visual routines—local, semi-independent operations that can engage mid- and higher-level processes (Ullman, 1987; Cavanagh et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on visual routines.

claim: A visual routine for causality could constitute a generalized mechanism that responds to all kinds of causal visual interactions.
source: In its purest form, such a visual routine could constitute a generalized mechanism that responds to all kinds of causal visual interactions.
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility being considered as one hypothesis.

claim: There could be many different specialized visual routines for the detection of causality that are tuned to the features of a particular causal interaction.
source: Alternatively, there could be many different specialized visual routines for the detection of causality that are tuned to the features of a particular causal interaction (e.g. the direction, kinematics, or object identity; Figure 1b; see Rips, 2011 for a discussion).
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical possibility being tested, with reference to Figure 1b and a citation.

claim: Observers perceive causality even in simple kinematic displays—a moving disc that stops next to another disc appears to launch the second disc into motion.
source: To this end, we took advantage of the phenomenon that observers perceive causality even in simple kinematic displays—a moving disc that stops next to another disc appears to launch the second disc into motion (i.e. launching effect, Figure 1c; Michotte, 1963; see Rips, 2011; Scholl and Tremoulet, 2000; White, 2006, White, 2017 for reviews).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on the launching effect and reference to Figure 1c.

claim: The prolonged viewing of launching events in an adaptation protocol strongly alters the perception of causality by reducing the proportion of reported launches in subsequent test events.
source: The prolonged viewing of such launching events in an adaptation protocol strongly alters the perception of causality by reducing the proportion of reported launches in subsequent test events (Rolfs et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work demonstrating this adaptation effect.

claim: The adaptation of causality is spatially specific to the retinotopic coordinates of the adapting stimulus.
source: The adaptation of causality is spatially specific to the retinotopic coordinates of the adapting stimulus (Kominsky and Scholl, 2020; Rolfs et al., 2013; for an object-centered elasticity aftereffect using a related stimulus on a circular motion path, see Arnold et al., 2015), suggesting that the detection of causal interactions is implemented locally in visual space.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating spatial specificity.

claim: The detection of causal interactions is implemented locally in visual space.
source: The adaptation of causality is spatially specific to the retinotopic coordinates of the adapting stimulus (Kominsky and Scholl, 2020; Rolfs et al., 2013; for an object-centered elasticity aftereffect using a related stimulus on a circular motion path, see Arnold et al., 2015), suggesting that the detection of causal interactions is implemented locally in visual space.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial specificity of adaptation effects.

claim: Visual adaptation to launches of a particular motion direction, motion speed, or feature identity transfers to other values of that feature space or is restricted to the feature values of the adaptor.
source: In three experiments, we assessed whether adaptation to launches of a particular motion direction, motion speed, or feature identity (i.e. a conjunction of two features) transfers to other values of that feature space or, alternatively, whether the consequences of adaptation are restricted to the feature values of the adaptor.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and research question being tested.

claim: The results provide compelling evidence for visual routines that are specialized for processing launches of a particular motion direction.
source: Our results provide compelling evidence for visual routines that are specialized for processing launches of a particular motion direction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Visual adaptation to launches successfully affected the perception of causality in Experiment 1.
source: Visual adaptation to launches successfully affected the perception of causality in this task.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Observers were less likely to report a launch after adapting to launches in the same direction as the test events.
source: That is, observers were less likely to report a launch after adapting to launches in the same direction as the test events (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: There was a significant main effect of event type (F (1, 7)=62.73, p<0.001) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launching than slip events.
source: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of event type (F (1, 7)=62.73, p<0.001; Figure 2a–c) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launching than slip events (ΔPSEevent = –0.11, CI95% = [–0.14–0.08]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Adaptors in a congruent direction as the test event resulted in stronger adaptation than in incongruent directions (F (1, 7)=41.62, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, adaptors in a congruent direction as the test event resulted in stronger adaptation than in incongruent directions (F (1, 7)=41.62, p<0.001; ΔPSEdirection = –0.11, CI95% = [–0.15–0.07]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant interaction (F (1, 7)=12.23, p=0.01), revealing that the influence of direction-congruency on the magnitude of adaptation was significantly stronger for launches than for slip events.
source: Critically, we observed a significant interaction (F (1, 7)=12.23, p=0.01), revealing that the influence of direction-congruency on the magnitude of adaptation was significantly stronger for launches than for slip events (Post-hoc t-test: t(7) = 3.50, p=0.01; ΔPSEeventXdirection = –0.09, CI95% = [–0.16–0.03]) supporting the hypothesis that specialized visual routines are tuned to the motion direction of launching events.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The significant interaction supports the hypothesis that specialized visual routines are tuned to the motion direction of launching events.
source: Critically, we observed a significant interaction (F (1, 7)=12.23, p=0.01), revealing that the influence of direction-congruency on the magnitude of adaptation was significantly stronger for launches than for slip events (Post-hoc t-test: t(7) = 3.50, p=0.01; ΔPSEeventXdirection = –0.09, CI95% = [–0.16–0.03]) supporting the hypothesis that specialized visual routines are tuned to the motion direction of launching events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results of the interaction effect.

claim: Both speed-congruent and speed-incongruent launches resulted in adaptation, demonstrating a transfer of adaptation across motion speeds.
source: Both speed-congruent (i.e. test events had the same speed as the adaptor) and speed-incongruent launches (i.e. test events and adaptor differed by a factor of 2) resulted in adaptation, demonstrating a transfer of adaptation across motion speeds (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 2d-f.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a significant main effect of event type (F (1, 7)=23.39, p=0.002) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launching than slip events.
source: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of event type (F (1, 7)=23.39, p=0.002; Figure 2d–f) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launching than slip events (ΔPSEevent = –0.14, CI95% = [–0.21–0.07]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The magnitude of adaptation was not significantly different for congruent and incongruent speed between adaptor and test event (F (1, 7)=3.43, p=0.107).
source: Importantly, the magnitude of adaptation was not significantly different for congruent and incongruent speed between adaptor and test event (F (1, 7)=3.43, p=0.107; ΔPSEspeed = 0.03 CI95% = [–0.01 0.07]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: There was no significant interaction between event type and speed (F (1, 7)=3.48, p=0.105) in Experiment 2.
source: Moreover, there was no significant interaction between event type and speed (F (1, 7)=3.48, p=0.105; ΔPSEeventXspeed = –0.06, CI95% = [–0.14 0.02]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The perception of causality is not tuned to motion speed—or, at least, that the tuning is very broad.
source: These findings demonstrate that the perception of causality is not tuned to motion speed—or, at least, that the tuning is very broad.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of speed-specific effects in Experiment 2.

claim: When one of the features in the feature conjunction differed, adaptation was observed only for test events in the same direction as the adaptor, irrespective of the object's color.
source: However, when one of the features in the feature conjunction differed, we observed adaptation only for test events in the same direction as the adaptor, irrespective of the object's color.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Color does not constitute a critical feature of the visual routine for detecting causal interactions.
source: Thus, color does not constitute a critical feature of the visual routine for detecting causal interactions (Figure 2g–i).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Experiment 3 shown in Figure 2g-i.

claim: In Experiment 3, there was a significant main effect of motion direction (F (1, 7)=21.07, p=0.003) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launches in the same as compared to the opposite direction as the adaptor.
source: The analysis revealed a significant main effect of motion direction (F (1, 7)=21.07, p=0.003) demonstrating stronger adaptation for launches in the same as compared to the opposite direction as the adaptor (ΔPSEdirection = –0.14, CI95% = [–0.22–0.07]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Adaptation following adaptors with the same color vs. different color assignments were not significantly different (F (1, 7)=0.071, p=0.798) in Experiment 3.
source: Adaptation following adaptors with the same color vs. different color assignments were not significantly different (F (1, 7)=0.071, p=0.798; ΔPSEcolor = –0.004, CI95% = [–0.03 0.03]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: There was a marginally significant interaction between color and motion direction (F (1, 7)=4.59, p=0.07) in Experiment 3.
source: However, we observed a marginally significant interaction between color and motion direction (F (1, 7)=4.59, p=0.07; ΔPSEdirectionXcolor = –0.07, CI95% = [–0.16 0.01]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Color had a marginally significant influence on the magnitude of adaptation when adaptor and test events were in same direction (t (7)=1.97, p=0.090).
source: Post-hoc paired t-tests showed that color had a marginally significant influence on the magnitude of adaptation when adaptor and test events were in same direction (t (7)=1.97, p=0.090; ΔPSEcolor_samedir = –0.04, CI95% = [–0.09 0.01]).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Color had no significant influence on the adaptation of causality when adaptor and test events were in opposite direction (t (7)=1.97, p=0.090).
source: However, color had no significant influence on the adaptation of causality when adaptor and test events were in opposite direction (t (7)=1.97, p=0.090; ΔPSEcolor_opp_dir = 0.03, CI95% = [–0.02 0.09]).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Visual routines underlie the perception of causality that are specialized for a launch's motion direction but invariant across a range of motion speeds.
source: Using visual adaptation, we revealed that visual routines underlie the perception of causality that are specialized for a launch's motion direction but invariant across a range of motion speeds.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data across all three experiments.

claim: The tuning of causal perception to motion direction reveals a mechanism that is operating locally in feature space.
source: The tuning of causal perception to motion direction reveals a mechanism that is operating locally in feature space and complements previous reports of a spatially specific mechanism residing in retinotopic space (Kominsky and Scholl, 2020; Rolfs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results combined with previous findings.

claim: The observed adaptation is specific to launching events that evoked a phenomenological impression of causality.
source: The observed adaptation is specific to launching events that evoked a phenomenological impression of causality.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison with slip events (non-causal control) in the experiments.

claim: Adapting simply to the direction of a moving stimulus will only change the input to the visual routine but not the functioning of the routine itself.
source: This implies that adapting simply to the direction of a moving stimulus will only change the input to the visual routine but not the functioning of the routine itself.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the specificity of adaptation to causal events.

claim: Motion direction constitutes a basic computational unit in vision and can be computed as early as in retinal circuits.
source: Motion direction constitutes a basic computational unit in vision and can be computed as early as in retinal circuits (e.g. in retinal ganglion cells about 2–3 synapses downstream of photoreceptors in rabbits, Barlow and Hill, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established work on motion direction computation in the retina.

claim: A retinal origin of launch detection is unlikely.
source: While a retinal origin of launch detection is unlikely, the specialization of visual routines for the perception of causality at the level of individual motion directions raises the possibility that this function is located surprisingly early in the visual system as opposed to a higher-level visual computation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the direction-selectivity findings.

claim: The specialization of visual routines for the perception of causality at the level of individual motion directions raises the possibility that this function is located surprisingly early in the visual system as opposed to a higher-level visual computation.
source: While a retinal origin of launch detection is unlikely, the specialization of visual routines for the perception of causality at the level of individual motion directions raises the possibility that this function is located surprisingly early in the visual system as opposed to a higher-level visual computation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the direction-selectivity findings.

claim: Adaptation at the category level of the causal interaction allows to distinguish specialized detectors for a particular causal interaction.
source: Thus, adaptation at the category level of the causal interaction allows to distinguish specialized detectors for a particular causal interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous adaptation studies on different causal interactions.

claim: Adaptation to triggering events transferred to launching events, but adaptation to entraining had no such influence.
source: While Michotte speculated about three separate causal impressions (i.e. launching, entraining, triggering; see White, 2017 for an extended catalog of causal interactions) adaptation helped to refine these categories as an adaptation to triggering events transferred to launching events, but adaptation to entraining had no such influence (Kominsky and Scholl, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Kominsky and Scholl (2020).

claim: Previous adaptation protocols demonstrated successful adaptation using adaptors with random motion direction.
source: While the present study demonstrates direction-selectivity for the detection of launches, previous adaptation protocols demonstrated successful adaptation using adaptors with random motion direction (Rolfs et al., 2013; Kominsky and Scholl, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The results suggest independent direction-specific routines, in which adaptation to launches in one direction does not counteract an adaptation to launches in the opposite direction.
source: These results, therefore, suggest independent direction-specific routines, in which adaptation to launches in one direction does not counteract an adaptation to launches in the opposite direction (as for example in opponent color coding).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current results combined with previous findings.

claim: Habituation studies in 6-mo-old infants demonstrated that the reversal of a launch resulted in a recovery from habituation to launches.
source: Habituation studies in 6-mo-old infants also demonstrated that the reversal of a launch resulted in a recovery from habituation to launches (while a non-causal control condition of delayed launches did not; Leslie and Keeble, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a habituation study in infants.

claim: In the infant study, the reversal of motion direction was accompanied by a reversal of the color assignment to the cause-effect-relationship.
source: In their study, the reversal of motion direction was accompanied by a reversal of the color assignment to the cause-effect-relationship.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used in the cited infant study.

claim: In adults, color does not play a major role in the detection of a launch.
source: In contrast, our findings suggest, that in adults color does not play a major role in the detection of a launch.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Experiment 3.

claim: The adaptation to triggering events (with a speed ratio of 1:3) resulted in significant retinotopic adaptation of ambiguous (launching) test events of different speed ratios.
source: This result complements a previous finding that reported that the adaptation to triggering events (with a speed ratio of 1:3) resulted in significant retinotopic adaptation of ambiguous (launching) test events of different speed ratios (i.e. test events with a speed ratio of 1:1 and of 1:3; Kominsky and Scholl, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The appearance of the objects in the launching event plays only a minor role in adapting the perception of causality (if any).
source: Indeed, our results show that the appearance of the objects in the launching event plays only a minor role in adapting the perception of causality (if any), suggesting that the visual system can calibrate the detection of causal interactions independent of the involved object identities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Experiment 3.

claim: The visual system can calibrate the detection of causal interactions independent of the involved object identities.
source: Indeed, our results show that the appearance of the objects in the launching event plays only a minor role in adapting the perception of causality (if any), suggesting that the visual system can calibrate the detection of causal interactions independent of the involved object identities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in Experiment 3.

claim: An event's spatiotemporal parameters mediate the perception of causality.
source: Our findings, therefore, provide additional support for the claim that an event's spatiotemporal parameters mediate the perception of causality (Michotte, 1963; Leslie, 1984; Scholl and Tremoulet, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current experimental data and citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: A direction-selective detection of launches allows adaptation to occur separately for each direction.
source: First, a direction-selective detection of launches allows adaptation to occur separately for each direction.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional benefit of direction-selective detection.

claim: The visual system can automatically calibrate the sensitivity of visual routines in response to real-world statistics.
source: That means that the visual system can automatically calibrate the sensitivity of these visual routines in response to real-world statistics.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional benefit of adaptation.

claim: Causal visual events are action-relevant, and the faster we can detect such causal interactions, the faster we can react to them.
source: Second, we think that causal visual events are action-relevant, and the faster we can detect such causal interactions, the faster we can react to them.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of causal detection.

claim: Direction-selective motion signals are available very early on in the visual system.
source: Direction-selective motion signals are available very early on in the visual system.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about visual processing.

claim: Visual routines that are based on direction-selective motion signals may enable faster detection.
source: Visual routines that are based on these direction-selective motion signals may enable faster detection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the functional benefit of using early motion signals.

claim: The present findings demonstrate direction-selectivity but do not pinpoint where exactly that visual routine is located.
source: While our present findings demonstrate direction-selectivity, they do not pinpoint where exactly that visual routine is located.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study.

claim: It is possible that the visual routine is located higher up in the visual system (or distributed across multiple levels), relying on a direction-selective population response as input.
source: It is possible that the visual routine is located higher up in the visual system (or distributed across multiple levels), relying on a direction-selective population response as input.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible neural implementations.

claim: The existence of specialized visual routines computing causality does not rule out the possibility of a more complex hierarchical architecture that is composed of both specialized and generalized routines.
source: The existence of specialized visual routines computing causality, however, does not rule out the possibility of a more complex hierarchical architecture that is composed of both specialized and generalized routines.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible architectures.

claim: The output of local, specialized detectors within that architecture could feed into a global, generalized detector.
source: The output of local, specialized detectors within that architecture could feed into a global, generalized detector.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible hierarchical processing.

claim: Visual adaptation to contrast sensitivity can yield weaker responses during early visual processing which are then passed on to other downstream areas.
source: Indeed, visual adaptation to other low-level visual features (e.g. contrast sensitivity) can yield weaker responses during early visual processing which are then passed on to other downstream areas (Kohn, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on visual adaptation.

claim: More complex behaviors of perceiving causal relations can result from integrating information across space, across time, and across sensory modalities.
source: However, we know that more complex behaviors of perceiving causal relations can result from integrating information across space (e.g. in causal capture; Scholl and Nakayama, 2002), across time (postdictive influence; Cavanagh et al., 2001), and across sensory modalities (Sekuler et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on multisensory integration and causal perception.

claim: Bayesian causal inference has been particularly successful as a normative framework to account for multisensory integration.
source: Bayesian causal inference has been particularly successful as a normative framework to account for multisensory integration (Körding et al., 2007; Shams and Beierholm, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on Bayesian causal inference.

claim: In the Bayesian framework, the evidence for a common-cause hypothesis competes with the evidence for an independent-causes hypothesis.
source: In that framework, the evidence for a common-cause hypothesis competes with the evidence for an independent-causes hypothesis (Shams and Beierholm, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation describing the Bayesian framework.

claim: The Bayesian framework emphasizes the distributed nature of the neural implementation for solving causal inferences, showing the contributions of parietal and frontal areas in addition to sensory processing.
source: This framework also emphasizes the distributed nature of the neural implementation for solving such inferences, showing the contributions of parietal and frontal areas in addition to sensory processing (for review see Shams and Beierholm, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on neural implementation of causal inference.

claim: Visual adaptation to contrast in mouse primary visual cortex is influenced by top-down factors such as behavioral relevance.
source: Moreover, even visual adaptation to contrast in mouse primary visual cortex is influenced by top-down factors such as behavioral relevance—suggesting a complex implementation of the observed adaptation results (Keller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on visual adaptation in mice.

claim: The present experiments presented purely visual events that do not require an integration across processing domains.
source: The present experiments, however, presented purely visual events that do not require an integration across processing domains.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The outcome of the suggested visual routine can provide initial evidence from within the visual system for a causal relation in the environment that may then be integrated with signals from other domains.
source: Thus, the outcome of our suggested visual routine can provide initial evidence from within the visual system for a causal relation in the environment that may then be integrated with signals from other domains (e.g. auditory signals).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about how the visual routine might contribute to broader causal inference.

claim: Perceived causality can be distinguished from judged causality.
source: Note, however, that perceived causality can be distinguished from judged causality: Even when participants are aware that a third variable (e.g. a color change) is the best predictor of the movement of the second disc in launching events, they still perceive the first disc as causing the movement of the second disc (Schlottmann and Shanks, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work distinguishing perception from judgment.

claim: Neurophysiological studies support the view of distributed neural processing underlying sensory causal interactions with the visual system playing a major role.
source: Neurophysiological studies support the view of distributed neural processing underlying sensory causal interactions with the visual system playing a major role.
evidence: This is a general statement about neurophysiological findings that will be elaborated with citations.

claim: Imaging studies revealed a network for the perception of causality that is also involved in action observation.
source: Imaging studies in particular revealed a network for the perception of causality that is also involved in action observation (Blakemore et al., 2003; Fonlupt, 2003; Fugelsang et al., 2005; Roser et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple imaging studies.

claim: The fact that visual adaptation of causality occurs in a retinotopic reference frame emphasizes the role of retinotopically organized areas within that network (e.g. V5 and the superior temporal sulcus).
source: The fact that visual adaptation of causality occurs in a retinotopic reference frame emphasizes the role of retinotopically organized areas within that network (e.g. V5 and the superior temporal sulcus).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the retinotopic specificity of adaptation.

claim: Single cell recordings in area F5 of the primate brain revealed that motor areas contribute to the perception of causality.
source: Interestingly, single cell recordings in area F5 of the primate brain revealed that motor areas contribute to the perception of causality (Caggiano et al., 2016; Rolfs, 2016), emphasizing the distributed nature of the computations underlying causal interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to single cell recording studies.

claim: The detection, and the prediction, of causality is essential for processes outside purely sensory systems (e.g. for understanding other's actions, for navigating, and for avoiding collisions).
source: This finding also stresses that the detection, and the prediction, of causality is essential for processes outside purely sensory systems (e.g. for understanding other's actions, for navigating, and for avoiding collisions).
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of causal detection.

claim: The neurophysiology subserving causal inference extends the candidate cortical areas that might contribute to the detection of causal relations, emphasizing the role of the frontal cortex for the flexible integration of multisensory representations.
source: The neurophysiology subserving in causal inference further extends the candidate cortical areas that might contribute to the detection of causal relations, emphasizing the role of the frontal cortex for the flexible integration of multisensory representations (Cao et al., 2019; Coen et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies on causal inference.

claim: Visual adaptation in general is thought to be one of the signatures of a perceptual process.
source: Visual adaptation in general is thought to be one of the signatures of a perceptual process (Hafri and Firestone, 2021) and, therefore, is informative for identifying the visual origin of a mechanism as opposed to, for instance, cognitive accounts (e.g. cognitive schema; see Rips, 2011 for a review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on visual adaptation as a marker of perception.

claim: An impression of causality emerges fast and automatically for briefly presented stimuli.
source: An impression of causality emerges fast and automatically for briefly presented stimuli (Michotte, 1963) and causal events reach awareness faster than non-causal events (Moors et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on the speed and automaticity of causal perception.

claim: Causal events reach awareness faster than non-causal events.
source: An impression of causality emerges fast and automatically for briefly presented stimuli (Michotte, 1963) and causal events reach awareness faster than non-causal events (Moors et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on awareness of causal events.

claim: The implementation of visual routines for the perception of causality in separate channels of a basic visual feature such as motion direction fortifies the view that our understanding of causal interactions indeed starts as a low-level perceptual routine.
source: The implementation of visual routines for the perception of causality in separate channels of a basic visual feature such as motion direction fortifies the view that our understanding of causal interactions indeed starts as a low-level perceptual routine.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In each of the three experiments, eight human observers were tested in five sessions.
source: In each of the three experiments, we tested eight human observers (Experiment 1: ages 21–32 y; five female; three male; eight right-handed; five right-eye dominant: Experiment 2: ages 21–30 y; five female; three male; seven right-handed; six right-eye dominant; Experiment 3: ages 23–30 y; six female; one non-binary; seven right-handed; six right-eye dominant) in five sessions (one training session without adaptation, four test sessions with adaptation).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The final sample size was determined by computing 90% power contours as a function of sample size and trial number and defining the additional criterion of a minimum of eight observers per experiment.
source: We determined the final sample size by computing 90% power contours as a function of sample size and trial number (Baker et al., 2021) and defining the additional criterion of a minimum of eight observers per experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the methods for determining sample size, with a citation.

claim: Observers who did not distinguish between passes and launches after the first session were excluded and replaced by new observers (resulting in the replacement of one observer in each experiment).
source: We excluded observers who did not distinguish between passes and launches after the first session and replaced them by new observers (resulting in the replacement of one observer in each experiment).
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria used in the experiments.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Psychology Department of the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and it followed the guidelines of the World Medical Association (2008) Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the Psychology Department of the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and it followed the guidelines of the World Medical Association (2008). Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval and compliance.

claim: Observers sat in a sound-shielded, dimly lit room putting their head on a chin and forehead rest.
source: Observers sat in a sound-shielded, dimly lit room putting their head on a chin and forehead rest.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Eye position was controlled by tracking observers' dominant eye using an Eyelink 1000 Desktop Mount eye tracker with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
source: We controlled for observers' eye position by tracking their dominant eye using an Eyelink 1000 Desktop Mount eye tracker (SR Research, Ottawa, ON, Canada) with a sampling rate of 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the eye tracking methods.

claim: Visual stimuli were displayed on a video-projection screen using a PROPixx DLP projector at a spatial resolution of 1920×1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz.
source: We displayed visual stimuli on a video-projection screen (Celexon HomeCinema, Tharston, Norwich, UK) using a PROPixx DLP projector (VPixx Technologies Inc, Saint Bruno, QC, Canada) at a spatial resolution of 1920×1080 pixels and a refresh rate of 120 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus presentation equipment.

claim: The screen was mounted on a wall at 180 cm away from the observer.
source: The screen was mounted on a wall at 180 cm away from the observer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The experiment was implemented in Matlab 2016b using the Psychophysics toolbox 3 for stimulus presentation and the Eyelink toolbox for control of the eye tracker.
source: The experiment was running on a DELL Precision T7810 (Debian GNU Linux 8) and implemented in Matlab 2016b (Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA) using the Psychophysics toolbox 3 (Brainard, 1997; Kleiner et al., 2007; Pelli, 1997) for stimulus presentation and the Eyelink toolbox (Cornelissen et al., 2002) for control of the eye tracker.
evidence: This is a description of the software used, with citations.

claim: In the test events, a peripheral disc approached a stationary second disc and stopped at varying disc overlaps across trials.
source: In the test events, a peripheral disc approached a stationary second disc and stopped at varying disc overlaps across trials (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: Immediately after the first disc stopped, the second disc started moving in the same direction and with the same speed as the first disc.
source: Immediately after that, the second disc started moving in the same direction and with the same speed as the first disc.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Demo trials of test events with 0% overlap are typically perceived as launches.
source: As part of the instructions, we presented short demo trials of test events with 0% overlap that are typically perceived as launches (see Video 1), and test events with full disc overlap, that are typically perceived as a pass (see Video 2).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in instructions, with reference to videos.

claim: Test events with full disc overlap are typically perceived as a pass.
source: As part of the instructions, we presented short demo trials of test events with 0% overlap that are typically perceived as launches (see Video 1), and test events with full disc overlap, that are typically perceived as a pass (see Video 2).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli used in instructions, with reference to videos.

claim: The entire duration of the test event was 175ms.
source: The entire duration of the test event was 175ms.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters.

claim: Observers reported whether they perceived a launch or a pass by pressing either the arrow up key for launches or arrow down key for passes.
source: At the end of the trial, observers reported whether they perceived a launch or a pass in the test event by pressing either the arrow up key for launches or arrow down key for passes.
evidence: This is a description of the response method.

claim: The method assumes that launches and passes can be mapped onto a dimension that ranges from causal to non-causal impressions.
source: In our study, we assessed causal perception by asking observers to report whether they observed a launch or a pass in events of varying ambiguity. This method assumes that launches and passes can be mapped onto a dimension that ranges from causal to non-causal impressions.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the assumptions underlying the method.

claim: It has been questioned whether pass events are a natural representative of non-causal events.
source: It has been questioned whether pass events are a natural representative of non-causal events: Observers often report high impressions of causality upon first exposure to pass events, which then decrease after seeing a canonical launch (Bechlivanidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work questioning the use of pass events.

claim: Participants completed a separate session that included canonical launches before starting the main experiment.
source: In our study, therefore, participants completed a separate session that included canonical launches before starting the main experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In Experiment 1, before the first trial of blocks 6-15, 320 launching events were presented at the same location as the test events.
source: Before the first trial of a block, we presented 320 launching events at the same location as the test events described above.
evidence: This is a description of the adaptation procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: The exact direction of the launching events in the adaptor was randomly chosen from a narrow uniform distribution around the direction on the horizontal meridian (±30 degrees).
source: The exact direction of these launching events was randomly chosen from a narrow uniform distribution around the direction on the horizontal meridian (±30 degrees).
evidence: This is a description of the adaptation procedure in Experiment 1.

claim: The long adaptation phase was complemented by a top-up adaptation of 16 launching events before each trial to maintain an effective adaptation across the entire block.
source: The long adaptation phase was complemented by a top-up adaptation of 16 launching events in the same direction as the adaptor (again drawn from the same narrow uniform distribution around that main direction) before each trial to maintain an effective adaptation across the entire block.
evidence: This is a description of the adaptation procedure.

claim: In slip events, the first peripheral disc moves towards a stationary disc, passes the stationary disc and stops only when it is adjacent to the opposite edge of the stationary disc.
source: In slip events, the first peripheral disc also moves towards a stationary disc. In contrast to launching events, however, the first disc passes the stationary disc and stops only when it is adjacent to the opposite edge of the stationary disc.
evidence: This is a description of the slip event stimuli used as control.

claim: Slip events do not elicit a causal impression.
source: While slip events do not elicit a causal impression, they have the same number of objects and motion onsets, the same motion direction and speed, as well as the same spatial area of the event as launches.
evidence: This is a description of the properties of slip events, based on established knowledge.

claim: Slip events have the same number of objects and motion onsets, the same motion direction and speed, as well as the same spatial area of the event as launches.
source: While slip events do not elicit a causal impression, they have the same number of objects and motion onsets, the same motion direction and speed, as well as the same spatial area of the event as launches.
evidence: This is a description of the control stimuli design.

claim: Each observer ran in a total of 1,680 trials in Experiment 1.
source: Overall, each observer ran in a total of 1,680 trials in Experiment 1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, adaptors and test events varied in motion speed either being the same as in Experiment 1 or half that speed.
source: In Experiment 2, we used a very similar design as in Experiment 1 with one notable difference. Adaptors and test events varied in motion speed either being the same as in Experiment 1 or half that speed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for Experiment 2.

claim: In slow events, the test event duration was twice as long (i.e. event duration of 350 ms) as for test events displayed at fast motion speed (i.e. event duration of 175 ms).
source: Correspondingly, in slow events, the test event duration was twice as long (i.e. event duration of 350 ms) as for test events displayed at fast motion speed (i.e. event duration of 175 ms).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters in Experiment 2.

claim: All test events (and adaptors) in Experiment 2 were always presented in the same direction (from left to right).
source: We presented all test events (and adaptors) always in the same direction (from left to right).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for Experiment 2.

claim: Each observer ran in a total of 1680 trials in Experiment 2.
source: Each observer ran in a total of 1680 trials in Experiment 2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 3, the two discs in the test events and during adaptation had different colors (i.e. red and green).
source: In Experiment 3, we determined the transfer of adaptation for feature conjunctions (motion direction x color). The two discs in the test events and during adaptation had different colors (i.e. red and green) and could move in both horizontal directions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for Experiment 3.

claim: The red and green discs were not matched for luminance.
source: The red and green discs were not matched for luminance.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus properties in Experiment 3.

claim: Measurements obtained after the experiments yielded a luminance of 21 cd/m2 for the green disc and 6 cd/m2 for the red disc.
source: Measurements obtained after the experiments yielded a luminance of 21 cd/m2 for the green disc and 6 cd/m2 for the red disc.
evidence: This is a description of the measured stimulus properties.

claim: In Experiment 3, slip events were not used as adaptors.
source: In contrast to Experiments 1 and 2, slip events were not used as adaptors.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for Experiment 3.

claim: Each observer ran in a total of 1,680 trials in Experiment 3.
source: Each observer ran in a total of 1,680 trials in Experiment 3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Disc overlap was related to the proportion of reported launches using logistic functions with four parameters for the intercept, slope, as well as upper and lower asymptotes.
source: We related disc overlap to the proportion of reported launches using logistic functions with four parameters for the intercept, slope, as well as upper and lower asymptotes.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: These functions were fitted separately for each observer and condition and obtained the points of subjective equality (PSE).
source: We fitted these functions separately for each observer and condition and obtained the points of subjective equality (PSE; the amount of overlap between the two discs in the test events that result in the same proportion of reported launches and passes).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: PSEs were analyzed using repeated-measures analyses of variance (rmANOVA).
source: For inferential statistics, we analyzed PSEs using repeated-measures analyses of variance (rmANOVA).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

claim: Neither of the studies reported in this article was preregistered.
source: Neither of the studies reported in this article was preregistered.
evidence: This is a statement about the study registration status.

claim: The data and analysis code has been deposited in the Open Science Framework and is publicly available at https://osf.io/x947m/.
source: The data and analysis code has been deposited in the Open Science Framework and is publicly available at https://osf.io/x947m/.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.
